Brick 7, step by step

This page shows, with short animations made for this course, everything your team does in Lab 07: one TDD (Test-Driven Development) cycle, the first code with its unit tests and their coverage, the black-box tables, the flow graph and its V(G) (cyclomatic complexity), the one-page test plan — then the hour at home. The full conditions are in the lab document; this page is the visual companion.

Time budget 1 – 2 – 11 h lecture · 2 h in class · 1 h at home — at most 3 hours of lab work (2 in class + 1 at home)
DeliverableYour code and its tests (one command runs them all) + /docs/07-testing.md, tag block7, link and tag on the LMS (Learning Management System)
DueSunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59 — recommended first version block7-draft by Sunday, November 8, 23:59, for feedback before the Mid-Term
Weight and outcome6.5 % of the course grade, the four Cs: Complete · Correct · Consistent · Clear — LO3 (Learning Outcome 3): the types of testing

The student schedule calls the bricks “Blocks” (Block 7 = Brick 7). Identifiers on this page: FR-nn (functional requirement number nn of Brick 5) · NFR-nn (non-functional requirement number nn) · UC-nn (use case number nn) · UT-nn (unit test number nn) · BB-nn (black-box test case number nn).

Every tool and technique here is open. The language, the test framework, the coverage tool, the editor, the drawing tool, the issue tracker, Git and the hosting site — each is a suggestion. Replace any of them, combine them, use your own technique (a decision table instead of partitions, a hand-drawn flow graph instead of Mermaid), or build your own tool — two examples are below. Research what you choose as an engineer would — who makes it, its licence and price, where it keeps your data, whether it will exist next year — and name it in section 0 of your file. Two limits only: the tests run with one command written in the file, and every link or download first passes the checklist of the Legal Notice. Starting points (official sites): Python with pytest, coverage.py and pytest-cov · Node.js with Jest or c8 · Java with JUnit, JaCoCo and Apache Maven · Visual Studio Code or any editor · Git and GitHub Issues or any tracker · Mermaid flowcharts.

Before you open a link or install anything, use the checklist of the Legal Notice, section 14 and Annex C: official sites only, links checked with VirusTotal, published checksums verified.

In class — Studio 1:10–2:50, wrap-up to 3:00

1

One TDD (Test-Driven Development) cycle

1:10–1:25 · 15 minutes · in class

  1. Open your code skeleton from the coached Studio of Class 6, or copy the starter for your language (Files). No skeleton yet? The starter is one.
  2. Run all the tests once:
    StarterOnceRun every test
    Pythonpython -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txtpython -m pytest
    JavaScriptnpm installnpm test
    Javaa Java Development Kit 17 or newer and Mavenmvn test
    Expected: five pass, one fails — UT-02, the test of slot_is_full(), is red on purpose. In Java the red test is counted as an error: the body throws an exception instead of returning a wrong value — still red.4
  3. Green. Write the simplest body that passes UT-02. Run the tests again: six pass.
  4. Refactor. Use the named constant instead of the number, read the names, run the tests again: still green. Commit with a message that says so.
  5. Now the same cycle on your product: the rule of one FR (functional requirement) of Brick 5 — its first test before the code, watch it fail, make it pass.

Done when: one red → green → refactor cycle on your own code is committed, with a commit message that says so.

Windows: if python is not found, use py (py -m pytest); a virtual environment works without activation through .venv\Scripts\python -m pytest.1

2

First code, at least six unit tests, coverage

1:25–2:00 · 35 minutes · in class

  1. In pairs, implement one or two core user stories — the rules first (the cohesive module that the controllers call, as in the design of Class 6), not the screens. One keyboard per pair; swap every 10 minutes.
  2. Write at least six unit tests in total: for each rule, one typical value, the values on its boundaries and one invalid input. Name every test after the behaviour (test_cancel_refused_nine_minutes_before_slot), and note the requirement it traces to.
  3. Run a coverage tool and record the statement and branch percentages and the lines not covered in section 3 of the file:
    • Python: python -m pytest --cov=<package> --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing
    • JavaScript: npm run coverage3
    • Java: mvn test — JaCoCo writes target/site/jacoco/index.html4

Coverage shows what was not tested; it never proves that a test checks the right result. 85 % with careful boundary tests is worth more than 100 % of happy paths — read what every test asserts.

Done when: six or more tests pass with one command, and the coverage numbers are in the file.

3

Black-box tables for two use cases

2:00–2:25 · 25 minutes · in class

  1. Choose two use cases of Brick 5 whose steps check a value — a limit, a time, a count. For each input, write the equivalence classes: the valid ones and at least one invalid one (beginners test only the happy path).
  2. Add the boundary values: each edge and the value just outside it, because mistakes such as > written instead of >= show up exactly there.
  3. One row per case in section 4, or in the black-box sheet 07-blackbox.csv: test identifier · input · partition · expected result. Leave actual and status for home.

Worked example — QueueLess, UC-04 Cancel order (FR-05). Input: minutes before the pick-up slot. Classes: invalid (< 0), too late (0–9), may cancel (≥ 10). Boundaries: −1, 0, 9, 10, 11, plus a typical 240. Six rows, BB-01 … BB-06. The sheet holds five more cases for UC-01 Place order (FR-03): −1, 0, 19, 20, 21.

Done when: two tables, each with at least one invalid class and its boundaries.

4

White-box: the flow graph and V(G) (cyclomatic complexity)

2:25–2:40 · 15 minutes · in class

  1. Pick the function of your code with the most decisions (if, elif, loops; and/or count too). Draw its flow graph on paper: one node per decision or block, one edge per possible flow. Split a compound condition such as a and b into one node per simple condition, so that the three computations agree.
  2. Compute V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) three ways — E − N + 2 (edges − nodes + 2), decisions + 1, regions of the graph — and check that they agree.
  3. List the basis paths and the unit test that covers each; write the missing tests now or at home.

Done when: the graph (photo or Mermaid text), the three computations and the path-to-test list are in section 5.

5

Test Plan v1

2:40–2:50 · 10 minutes · in class

Fill the one-page table of section 1 — you fill the template; you do not design it:

  1. Scope — what is tested in this version, and what is not (name it).
  2. Types of testing — who and when, the five of LO3 (Learning Outcome 3): a unit test checks one function or class alone; an integration test checks that parts work together; a system test checks the whole deployed product against the requirements; a user acceptance test lets real users confirm that it meets their need; a performance test checks behaviour under load. The first four are also called test levels; performance testing is a non-functional test type, usually run on the whole system. Today you write unit tests and plan the other four.
  3. Tools — the framework, the coverage tool, where results are kept.
  4. Entry criteria — when testing of a feature may start; exit criteria — when a version is good enough to tag.
  5. Defect process — where defects go (for example GitHub Issues) and the labels bug, severity, priority.

Done when: all six parts have one or two lines.

2:50

Wrap-up

2:50–3:00 · 10 minutes · in class

The professor shows the Brick 7 box and the December 20 deadline. Exit ticket, one line on paper: “Your coverage %, your V(G) (cyclomatic complexity), and the type of testing you find hardest to explain.” Commit before you leave:

git add .
git commit -m "Brick 7: first code, unit tests, black-box tables, flow graph - in-class draft"

At home — 60 minutes, maximum

6–8

Run the cases, record the defects, trace, count

40 minutes · at home

  1. Step 6 (15 min): run every black-box case — by hand in the running product, or as a unit test — and fill actual and status. Every failure becomes a defect: an issue with a one-line title, the steps, the expected and the actual result, the label bug, a severity (how bad the effect is) and a priority (how soon it must be fixed). If you fix it, add the test that exposed it, so it can never come back unseen.6
  2. Step 7 (15 min): fill the test column of your Brick 5 traceability matrix (section 7): every implemented FR (functional requirement) gets at least one unit or black-box test identifier; one with no test is planned for a later type of testing (say which: integration, system, user acceptance or performance) or is a gap. Then read Bricks 3 and 5 beside Brick 7 and fix one inconsistency.
  3. Step 8 (10 min): section 8 — tests passing out of total, statement and branch coverage, V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) of your function, and defect density = defects ÷ KLOC (thousands of lines of code). Count your lines with any line counter and show the division.

Done when: actual and status are filled, defects are issues (or one test gap is recorded), the test column is filled and the numbers are in one table.

9

Commit, tag, push, post

10 minutes · at home

  1. Commit and push the code, the tests and the file: git add . → git commit -m "…" → git push.5
  2. git push does not send tags, so each tag is pushed by name. Optional first version for feedback (recommended by Sunday, November 8, 23:59): git tag block7-draft then git push origin block7-draft.
  3. Graded version — tag it last, when the brick is final, by Sunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59: git tag block7 then git push origin block7. Changed something after tagging? git tag -f block7 and git push --force origin block7. If only block7-draft exists on December 20, that version is graded.
  4. Check the tag on the hosting site (on GitHub: Releases → Tags).6 Then post the repository link and the tag name on the LMS (Learning Management System).8

Declare any AI (Artificial Intelligence) tool in section 0 of your file — which tool, for what — and keep every name and every piece of test data fictional: Legal Notice, sections 6.7, 18.1 and 18.2.

10

Read and memorise

10 minutes · at home

  • Pressman and Maxim, Software Engineering: A Practitioner's Approach, 9th edition (McGraw Hill): skim chapters 19 (component-level testing) and 20 (integration-level testing) for the parts you did not use today; the rest is weekly reading, outside this hour.
  • The flash-cards of the week: verification · validation · unit test · integration test · system test · user acceptance test · performance test · equivalence partition · boundary value · cyclomatic complexity · statement coverage · TDD (Test-Driven Development) · stub / mock · defect density.
  • Optional, outside the three hours and never graded: the four Numbers exercises of the schedule in /docs/numbers.md.

That is the hour. If you are past it, stop: what is missing becomes a question for the finishing workshops of December.

Build your own tool — two possible examples

The lab invites you to build tools. Here are two short Python scripts, each with a comment before every line saying what the line does and why. Use them, rewrite them in another language, or design something different — and name your choice in section 0 of your file. Both run on any Python 3 from python.org; they need nothing else.1

1 · A V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) counter

Task: print every function of a Python file with its number of decisions and its V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = decisions + 1. Relation to the lab: Step 4 computes it by hand three ways; this is a fourth way that checks your graph.

# =============================================================================
# CS 330 · Lab 07 / Brick 7 — build your own tool: a V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) counter
# TASK. Print, for every function of a Python file, its number of decisions and its
# V(G) = decisions + 1, so that Step 4 can check the hand-drawn flow graph.
# RELATION TO THE LAB. Step 4 computes V(G) three ways by hand; this script is a
# fourth, automatic way. When it disagrees with your graph, find out who is wrong.
# One possible version among many: rewrite it, extend it, or build a different tool.
# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub © 2026, governed by the Legal Notice:
# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
# =============================================================================

# ast is Python's own parser: it turns source code into a tree of statements and expressions.
import ast
# sys gives access to the command-line arguments (the file to analyse).
import sys

# These nodes each add one decision: if/elif, the two loops, a conditional expression, an except clause.
DECISION_NODES = (ast.If, ast.For, ast.AsyncFor, ast.While, ast.IfExp, ast.ExceptHandler)
# These nodes start a new function or class; their decisions belong to them, not to the outer function.
NEW_SCOPE = (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef, ast.ClassDef, ast.Lambda)


# count_decisions() walks the children of one node and returns how many decisions they contain.
def count_decisions(node):
    # The running total of decisions found below this node.
    total = 0
    # Visit every direct child of the node (statements, expressions, clauses).
    for child in ast.iter_child_nodes(node):
        # A nested function or class is measured on its own, so skip its body here.
        if isinstance(child, NEW_SCOPE):
            # Go on with the next child.
            continue
        # if, elif, for, while, x if c else y, except: one decision each.
        if isinstance(child, DECISION_NODES):
            # Add the decision.
            total += 1
        # "a and b and c" holds two operators: each and / or is one more decision.
        elif isinstance(child, ast.BoolOp):
            # Three operands means two operators, so add operands minus one.
            total += len(child.values) - 1
        # A comprehension such as [x for x in xs if x > 0] loops (one decision) and may filter.
        elif isinstance(child, ast.comprehension):
            # One for the loop, plus one for every if filter inside it.
            total += 1 + len(child.ifs)
        # Then look deeper: decisions can be nested inside this child.
        total += count_decisions(child)
    # Report the total to the caller.
    return total


# main() reads the file named on the command line and prints one line per function.
def main():
    # Use the first argument as the file name; without one, measure the starter's rules module.
    path = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "queueless/orders.py"
    # Open the file as text in UTF-8, the encoding of Python source files.
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as source:
        # Parse the whole file into a syntax tree; a syntax error stops here with a clear message.
        tree = ast.parse(source.read(), filename=path)
    # Print the header of the result table.
    print(f"{'function':<28}{'line':>6}{'decisions':>11}{'V(G)':>6}")
    # Visit every node of the tree, in no particular order.
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        # Only functions (normal and async) are measured.
        if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
            # Count the decisions of this function's own body.
            decisions = count_decisions(node)
            # Print name, line number, decisions and V(G) = decisions + 1.
            print(f"{node.name:<28}{node.lineno:>6}{decisions:>11}{decisions + 1:>6}")


# Run main() only when the file is started as a script, not when it is imported.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Start the tool.
    main()

# =============================================================================
# STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION
# 1. ast.parse() reads the code the way Python itself does, so comments and strings
#    that contain the word "if" are never counted by mistake.
# 2. count_decisions() adds one for every if/elif, loop, conditional expression and
#    except clause, and one for every extra and/or operand — the rule of Step 4.
# 3. Nested functions are skipped inside their parent and measured on their own line.
# 4. V(G) = decisions + 1 is the number of basis paths: one test per basis path
#    executes both outcomes of every decision (sometimes fewer tests also do).
# 5. Not counted in this short version: match/case statements. Extending it is a good
#    first change — and a test for your own tool is a good second one.
# =============================================================================

Run it in the Python starter folder: python vg_count.py queueless/orders.py (on Windows, py vg_count.py queueless\orders.py). It prints:

function                      line  decisions  V(G)
can_cancel                      27          1     2
slot_is_full                    37          0     1
pickup_status                   45          3     4

pickup_status() has V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = 4 — the same number as the flow graph of Step 4. Before Step 1 is done, slot_is_full() has no decision (V(G) = 1); after it, still none: a comparison that returns its result is not a branch.

2 · Black-box sheet → Markdown table

Task: turn the black-box sheet (a CSV (comma-separated values) file) into the table of section 4, with a pass / fail / not-run count. Relation to the lab: Steps 3 and 6 fill the sheet; the script keeps the file and the sheet identical.

# =============================================================================
# CS 330 · Lab 07 / Brick 7 — build your own tool: black-box sheet → Markdown table
# TASK. Read the black-box sheet (a CSV — comma-separated values — file) and print
# the table of section 4 of /docs/07-testing.md, with a pass / fail / not-run count.
# RELATION TO THE LAB. Steps 3 and 6 fill the sheet; this script turns it into the
# Markdown table, so the file and the sheet never disagree.
# One possible version among many: rewrite it, extend it, or build a different tool.
# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub © 2026, governed by the Legal Notice:
# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
# =============================================================================

# csv reads comma-separated files correctly, including commas inside quoted cells.
import csv
# sys gives access to the command-line arguments (the sheet to convert).
import sys

# The columns of the sheet to keep, in order, each as (heading in the sheet, short heading in the file).
COLUMNS = [
    # The identifier of the case and the value given to the program.
    ("Test identifier", "Test identifier"), ("Input", "Input"),
    # The equivalence class (partition) that the input belongs to.
    ("Partition (valid / invalid)", "Partition"),
    # What the requirement says must happen, and what really happened in the run.
    ("Expected result", "Expected"), ("Actual result", "Actual"),
    # pass or fail, written after the run (Step 6).
    ("Status (pass / fail)", "Status"),
    # The closing bracket ends the list.
]


# cell() makes one value safe for a Markdown table.
def cell(text):
    # A vertical bar would end the cell early, so escape it; strip spaces at both ends.
    return (text or "").strip().replace("|", "\\|")


# main() reads the sheet and prints the Markdown table followed by a short count.
def main():
    # Use the first argument as the file name; without one, read the lab's template.
    path = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "07-blackbox.csv"
    # Open the sheet; newline="" lets the csv module handle line endings itself.
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as sheet:
        # Read every row as a dictionary keyed by the column headings of the first line.
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(sheet))
    # Print the heading row of the Markdown table.
    print("| " + " | ".join(short for _, short in COLUMNS) + " |")
    # Print the separator row that Markdown requires under the headings.
    print("|" + "---|" * len(COLUMNS))
    # Prepare the three counters of the summary line.
    passed, failed, not_run = 0, 0, 0
    # Handle the cases one by one, in the order of the sheet.
    for row in rows:
        # Print the kept columns of this case as one table row.
        print("| " + " | ".join(cell(row.get(name)) for name, _ in COLUMNS) + " |")
        # Read the status in lower case, so "Pass" and "pass" count alike.
        status = cell(row.get("Status (pass / fail)")).lower()
        # A case marked pass increases the pass counter.
        if status == "pass":
            # Count it.
            passed += 1
        # A case marked fail increases the fail counter: it needs an issue number.
        elif status == "fail":
            # Count it.
            failed += 1
        # An empty status means the case has not been run yet.
        else:
            # Count it.
            not_run += 1
    # Print an empty line, then the summary that goes under the table.
    print()
    # The counts make Step 8 quicker: the number of cases and how many still wait.
    print(f"{len(rows)} cases: {passed} pass, {failed} fail, {not_run} not run yet.")


# Run main() only when the file is started as a script, not when it is imported.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Start the tool.
    main()

# =============================================================================
# STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION
# 1. csv.DictReader() reads each line of the sheet as a dictionary, using the
#    headings of the first line as keys, so the column order of the sheet may change.
# 2. COLUMNS chooses the six columns of section 4 and their short headings.
# 3. cell() escapes the vertical bar, the one character that breaks a Markdown table.
# 4. The counters turn the status column into the summary line for Step 8.
# 5. Paste the output into section 4 of /docs/07-testing.md, or redirect it:
#    python blackbox_to_md.py docs/07-blackbox.csv > docs/07-blackbox-table.md
# =============================================================================

Run it next to the sheet: python blackbox_to_md.py 07-blackbox_TEMPLATE.csv. On the empty template the last line reads 10 cases: 0 pass, 0 fail, 10 not run yet.

Version notes

Everything shown was checked on October 25, 2026. If a newer version of a site or program looks or behaves differently, follow its official documentation.

  1. Python. The current release was 3.15.1, published October 21, 2026; 3.15.0 came out on October 9, and 3.14 is still maintained (python.org — downloads). pytest 9 needs Python 3.10 or newer, and the current coverage.py (7.17) needs 3.11 — on 3.10, pip simply installs an older coverage.py. The two tools on this page run on any Python 3. On Windows, the launcher py replaces python when the latter is not found.
  2. pytest and coverage. pytest 9.1.1, pytest-cov 7.1.0 and coverage.py 7.17.0 were the current versions (pytest · pytest-cov · coverage.py). The animations show real output of those versions; the timings (0.02 s, 0.06 s) and the exact spacing of the coverage table change from machine to machine and between versions — the columns Stmts, Miss, Branch, BrPart, Cover and Missing have been stable for years.
  3. Jest and Node.js. Jest 30.5.2 was current (jestjs.io); its coverage table has the columns % Stmts, % Branch, % Funcs, % Lines and Uncovered Line #s, so it looks different from the Python one. Node.js 26 (26.12.1) was the “Current” line and becomes the long-term-support line on October 28, 2026; 24 and 22 are maintained long-term-support lines (Node.js release schedule). The JavaScript starter was run on Node.js 22. c8 (12.0.0) measures coverage for Node.js's own test runner, if you prefer it to Jest.
  4. Java. The starter uses JUnit 6.1.3 (junit.org — JUnit 6 needs Java 17 or newer), JaCoCo 0.8.15 (jacoco.org) and the Maven Surefire plugin 3.6.0; Java 25 is the current long-term-support release. Maven downloads JUnit and JaCoCo the first time you run mvn test, so run it once at home or before the lab. A test that throws an unexpected exception is reported as an error (Errors: 1), not a failure.
  5. Git. The current release was 2.56.0, published September 28, 2026 (git-scm.com). The commands used here have been stable for many years; the wording of Git's messages can differ slightly between versions. Why tags need their own push: Pro Git, “Tagging”.
  6. GitHub. Tags are listed under Releases → Tags (GitHub Docs — Viewing tags). The label bug exists in every new repository; create severity: 1 … severity: 3 and priority: high / medium / low once, under Issues → Labels (GitHub Docs — Managing labels · Creating an issue). GitHub changes its interface often; GitLab, Codeberg and other hosts use their own menus.
  7. Mermaid. The documentation showed Mermaid 12.2.0 (Mermaid — flowchart syntax). GitHub draws Mermaid charts inside Markdown (GitHub Docs — Creating diagrams) but may run a different version; writing info in a Mermaid block shows which. A photo of a hand-drawn graph is accepted.
  8. The course site. Each institution's LMS (Learning Management System) looks different; post exactly the repository link and the tag name.
  9. About the animations. All seven were drawn for this course with a short program. The terminal texts are real outputs recorded on October 25, 2026 (pytest 9.1.1, pytest-cov 7.1.0, Git on a local test repository), with paths shortened; the issue, the tracker and the hosting-site views are schematic. Team Falcon, QueueLess and all data are fictional.

No vendor, standards body, platform or institution named here is affiliated with Cyber.SoHo (section 5). Course materials are licensed for study only — do not repost them (section 4); your own code remains yours (18.3). The student acknowledgement form (Annex A, e-signature) is provided separately.

  • Standards and terms: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1:2022 (joint software-testing standard of the International Organization for Standardization, the International Electrotechnical Commission and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers — part 1, general concepts) · ISTQB (International Software Testing Qualifications Board) — its Glossary.
  • Origins: Thomas J. McCabe, A Complexity Measure, 1976 — the paper (publisher record) · Kent Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example, 2002 — publisher's page (InformIT).
  • Textbook: Pressman & Maxim, 9th edition — McGraw Hill, chapters 19 and 20.
